EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance Benchmark for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven Coding Systems

Wentao Zhang1,† ,\mathpunct{,} Jianfeng Wang2,† ,\mathpunct{,} Liheng Liang3,† ,\mathpunct{,} Yilei Zhao1 ,\mathpunct{,} HaiBin Wen4 ,\mathpunct{,} Zhe Zhao5,‡
1 Nanyang Technological University 2 East China University of Science and Technology
3 Guangdong Ocean University 4 City University of Hong Kong 5 Stanford University
zhangwent963@gmail.com, ehz0002@stanford.edu
Abstract.

As large language models (LLMs) continue to advance in programming tasks, LLM-driven coding systems have evolved from one-shot code generation into complex systems capable of iterative improvement during inference. However, existing code benchmarks primarily emphasize static correctness and implicitly assume fixed model capability during inference. As a result, they do not capture inference-time self-evolution, such as whether accuracy and efficiency improve as an agent iteratively refines its solutions. They also provide limited accounting of resource costs and rarely calibrate model performance against that of human programmers. Moreover, many benchmarks are dominated by high-resource languages, leaving cross-language robustness and long-tail language stability underexplored. Therefore, we present EvoCodeBench, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving LLM-driven coding systems across programming languages with direct comparison to human performance. EvoCodeBench tracks performance dynamics, measuring solution correctness alongside efficiency metrics such as solving time, memory consumption, and improvement algorithmic design over repeated problem-solving attempts. To ground evaluation in a human-centered reference frame, we directly compare model performance with that of human programmers on the same tasks, enabling relative performance assessment within the human ability distribution. Furthermore, EvoCodeBench supports multiple programming languages, enabling systematic cross-language and long-tail stability analyses under a unified protocol. Our results demonstrate that self-evolving systems exhibit measurable gains in efficiency over time, and that human-relative and multi-language analyses provide insights unavailable through accuracy alone. EvoCodeBench establishes a foundation for evaluating coding intelligence in evolving LLM-driven systems.

Code Benchmark, Self-Evolving Agents, LLM-Driven Coding Systems, Human Performance Comparison, Programming Languages

1. Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have progressed from code-completion utilities to general-purpose programming assistants and building blocks for agentic coding systems. In contrast to one-shot code generation, contemporary agents can self-evolve during inference by iteratively refining candidate programs, repairing failures using execution feedback, and reusing intermediate artifacts, tools, or memory to improve both correctness and efficiency within the same problem-solving process. This shift motivates a central evaluation challenge: how should coding competence be measured when behavior is adaptive at inference time and performance is jointly determined by solution quality, resource cost, and improvement dynamics? Early benchmarks such as HumanEval (Chen, 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), and APPS (Hendrycks et al., 2021) standardized evaluation by measuring functional correctness via unit tests under fixed specifications, while competition-level datasets such as CodeContests (Li et al., 2022) further raised the difficulty ceiling. Subsequent work strengthened test suites (Liu et al., 2023a), increased freshness via continuously updated algorithmic tasks (LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2024)), and addressed repository-level software engineering settings (SWE-Bench (Jimenez et al., 2023)), while recent extensions broaden coverage across languages and incorporate efficiency-oriented signals such as execution cost and resource overhead (Raihan et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Qing et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024). However, a coherent framework for evaluating inference-time self-evolution in coding agents remains underdeveloped.

Despite these advances, existing benchmarks exhibit three limitations when applied to LLM-based coding systems, including one-shot models and agentic systems that self-evolve during inference. First, the prevailing paradigm remains static and benchmarks treat problems as independent one-shot instances and score systems primarily by final correctness, which obscures inference-time dynamics. Recent methods such as Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) and Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) demonstrate that iterative refinement can substantially boost pass rates, yet existing benchmarks rarely quantify whether a system becomes more accurate and efficient within the inference process, how quickly it improves as it refines solutions, or what time and memory costs are incurred, so they cannot distinguish fast, reliable solvers from systems that succeed only after expensive trial-and-error (Olausson et al., 2023). Second, results are typically reported in absolute accuracy units with limited calibration to human performance. Without human-referenced metrics, it is difficult to interpret what a given pass rate implies about practical coding competence or to report where a system falls on a human-calibrated scale, including its percentile rank or the number of humans it outperforms on the same tasks. Third, multilingual coverage is often dominated by a single language and ecosystem (often Python), which can mask cross-language generalization and bias evaluation toward familiar tooling and idioms. Although multilingual benchmarks such as MultiPL-E (Cassano et al., 2023) have extended evaluation to many languages, they still lack efficiency and human-referential metrics. This imbalance is especially problematic under long-tail usage patterns. According to the TIOBE Index for January 2026, Python accounts for 22.61% and Kotlin accounts for 0.97% (TIOBE Software BV, 2026). Such market skew can translate into differences in the amount of training data available per language, potentially inducing systematic bias in LLMs, yet existing benchmarks rarely measure or diagnose this effect.

We introduce EvoCodeBench to address these gaps with an evaluation framework for LLM-driven coding systems, including both one-shot models and self-evolving agents. EvoCodeBench evaluates systems on competitive-programming-style problems in multiple mainstream languages (e.g., Python, C++, Java, Go, and Kotlin), and it is designed to capture inference-time improvement rather than only final outcomes. Beyond pass rate, EvoCodeBench records efficiency and resource usage signals, including wall-clock solving time, memory consumption, and improvement trajectories as the system solves problems during inference. We pair these measurements with platform-side judging in a standardized execution environment, which returns acceptance status and fine-grained performance feedback such as runtime, memory usage, and percentile-based beats statistics, enabling analyses of whether gains in correctness come with disproportionate cost. We also provide standardized evaluation scripts and reporting templates to facilitate reproducibility and fair comparisons across model families and agent configurations. Finally, EvoCodeBench enables human-referenced reporting by situating model performance within the distribution of human submissions on the same tasks, including percentile ranks and the number of human solutions a system outperforms. Specifically, we make the following contributions:

  • •

    We present the first systematic, human-referenced evaluation of LLM-based coding systems, situating model performance within the empirical distribution of human submissions and enabling interpretable comparisons in terms of percentile rank and the number of humans a system outperforms.

  • •

    We reformulate coding evaluation from a static, endpoint-focused paradigm to a trajectory-level analysis that jointly characterizes correctness, efficiency, and resource cost during inference-time self-evolution, and we empirically validate the necessity and stability of this evaluation framework across multiple languages, including long-tail programming ecosystems.

  • •

    We release EvoCodeBench, a large-scale multilingual benchmark with standardized judging, human baselines, and reproducible evaluation protocols, and demonstrate how its metrics provide actionable insights for the design and future development of coding LLMs and agentic systems.

2. Related Work

2.1. Evaluating LLMs on Isolated Coding Tasks

Early benchmarks for evaluating LLMs on programming tasks primarily emphasize static correctness on small, self-contained problems. Representative datasets such as HumanEval (Chen, 2021) and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) assess whether a generated function satisfies a predefined specification by passing a fixed suite of unit tests, while APPS (Hendrycks et al., 2021) and CodeContests (Li et al., 2022) raise the difficulty ceiling to competitive-programming-level challenges with thousands of problems. Subsequent variants with strengthened test suites, including HumanEval Pro and MBPP Pro (Yu et al., 2024) and EvalPlus (Liu et al., 2023a), further tighten correctness criteria to better discriminate among strong models. These benchmarks have played a central role in standardizing evaluation protocols for functional code generation and tracking rapid progress in model capabilities.

However, these evaluations largely assume fixed model behavior during inference and treat each problem as an independent one-shot instance. Consequently, they provide limited visibility into inference-time self-evolution, even though methods such as Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) and Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) have shown that iterative refinement can substantially improve pass rates, and analyses of self-repair (Olausson et al., 2023) highlight the need to account for computational cost when evaluating such gains. To address concerns about data contamination and task realism, later benchmarks such as LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2024) curate continuously updated algorithmic problems sourced from competitive programming platforms and evaluate auxiliary skills such as self-repair and test-output prediction. Despite improvements in data freshness and diversity, the dominant paradigm remains centered on final correctness on fixed tasks and offers limited calibration to human performance or systematic characterization of inference-time efficiency dynamics.

2.2. Benchmarking LLM-Driven Coding Systems

Beyond isolated function synthesis, recent work has increasingly shifted toward evaluating LLM-based agents and more complex coding systems in realistic software engineering settings. Repository-level benchmarks assess a model’s ability to resolve real-world issues through multi-file code edits, dependency reasoning, and test-driven validation, marking an important step toward capturing practical workflows (Jimenez et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023b). Class-level benchmarks such as ClassEval (Du et al., 2024) move beyond function-level evaluation to assess generation of interdependent code units, while broader task suites like BigCodeBench (Zhuo et al., 2024) evaluate diverse function-call composition across libraries. In parallel, agent-oriented benchmarks investigate multi-step reasoning, tool use, and interaction (Liu et al., 2023c; Guo et al., 2024; Mialon et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2024), and multi-agent frameworks such as MapCoder (Islam et al., 2024) demonstrate that decomposing the code generation pipeline into specialized agents can improve competitive-programming performance.

More recent extensions expand evaluation along additional dimensions such as multilingual coverage and efficiency awareness by examining cross-language generalization (Cassano et al., 2023; Ding et al., 2023; Raihan et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025) and incorporating execution cost, runtime performance, or memory overhead into evaluation protocols (Huang et al., 2024; Qing et al., 2025). However, these extensions primarily add new axes without fundamentally revising the underlying evaluation target. Even when efficiency signals are reported, they are rarely integrated with inference-time adaptation and improvement dynamics, and multilingual coverage is often dominated by high-resource languages, leaving long-tail stability underexplored.

2.3. Limitations of Existing Benchmarks

Across both isolated coding benchmarks and agent-oriented evaluation frameworks, a common limitation persists. Even as state-of-the-art models approach performance saturation on strengthened algorithmic benchmarks (e.g., HumanEval Pro and MBPP Pro) and demonstrate competitive results on realistic software engineering tasks (e.g., SWE-Bench subsets), there is no established framework that jointly measures inference-time self-evolution, efficiency, and human-relative capability. In particular, existing benchmarks provide limited human-referenced metrics, which constrains the interpretability of claims about human-level or superhuman coding ability. Moreover, they do not explicitly characterize whether systems become faster or more accurate during inference as they refine solutions (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023), nor do they systematically link such improvements to time and memory costs. Finally, language coverage remains skewed toward high-resource languages, and market-level usage skew can translate into training-data imbalance and language bias (TIOBE Software BV, 2026), yet benchmarks rarely quantify this effect. These gaps motivate the need for an evaluation framework that jointly models performance dynamics, efficiency, human-relative capability, and cross-language stability, which we address in EvoCodeBench.

3. EvoCodeBench

3.1. Benchmark Design Rationale

Our benchmark construction is driven by the three motivations outlined above, namely evaluating inference-time self-evolution, calibrating performance against human ability, and assessing cross-language robustness under long-tail language usage. To this end, we build EvoCodeBench on top of the LeetCode online judge, which provides an execution-based evaluation interface and rich feedback signals that closely match our requirements. Specifically, acceptance status and pass rate, together with the number of passed test cases for partially correct submissions, enable fine-grained assessment of functional correctness beyond binary success. For accepted submissions, the platform reports runtime and memory usage, along with percentile-based runtime beats and memory beats statistics computed against the distribution of human submissions, which directly supports human-referenced evaluation. Finally, LeetCode provides standardized starter code across many programming languages, enabling consistent multi-language evaluation and the study of long-tail language stability under a unified measurement protocol. These signals also facilitate analyzing efficiency–accuracy trade-offs and identifying failure modes that emerge only under constrained runtime or memory budgets.

3.2. Benchmark Construction

Data Collection. We collect problems through the SQL interface provided by LeetCode and retrieve the full set of 3,822 programming problems available at the time of crawling. For each problem, we extract the full natural-language statement and normalize it into a structured representation that preserves key semantic elements, including embedded images when present, as well as the official input–output examples. We store image links and resolve them to local assets so that models can be evaluated with the same visual context as human solvers. In addition, we collect language-specific starter code templates for a broad set of languages, enabling consistent prompt construction and fair cross-language comparison. Each problem is further annotated with its platform-provided difficulty label (Easy, Medium, and Hard) and a set of topical tags that describe the required algorithmic concepts and data structures, such as arrays, trees, dynamic programming, mathematics, and strings. During ingestion, we perform basic quality checks, including filtering malformed records, removing duplicates, and validating that problem statements, examples, and templates are successfully parsed. Figure 2 summarizes tag and difficulty distributions, used to guide dataset balancing and analyze performance variation across problem categories and difficulty strata.

Problem Characteristics. LeetCode-style algorithmic problems provide a controlled yet demanding setting for evaluating coding competence in both one-shot LLMs and LLM-based agents. Each task specifies explicit constraints and input–output behavior that must be matched exactly, stressing instruction following, edge-case coverage, and implementation fidelity under a fixed interface. The breadth of tags and difficulty levels further tests algorithm selection, data-structure proficiency, and complexity-aware reasoning, while requiring robust translation from high-level ideas to executable code. Because evaluation is execution-based, brittle solutions are reliably exposed through concrete failures such as off-by-one errors, corner-case bugs, and language-specific pitfalls. Standardized starter templates across languages enable systematic cross-language comparisons, including robustness in long-tail languages with distinct syntax and runtime characteristics. Finally, since many problems admit within-inference refinement, this setting probes agentic behaviors such as self-repair, hypothesis testing against examples, and efficiency-aware optimization under runtime and memory budgets.

Problem Evaluation. We adopt a unified evaluation protocol that standardizes model interaction with the execution environment through a lightweight vanllia coding agent, enabling fair and reproducible comparison across foundation models. For each problem instance, the agent presents a fixed input representation to the model and deterministically extracts executable source code from the model’s output. The code is then submitted to an official execution-based judging service, which evaluates functional correctness on hidden test cases and reports resource usage statistics. This design ensures that all models are assessed under identical input formats, execution conditions, and scoring criteria.

To capture inference-time self-evolution, we further introduce a self-evolving coding agent that allows models to iteratively refine their solutions within a single problem-solving episode. Under a fixed revision budget, the agent supports multiple rounds of solution updates while keeping the task specification, prompt structure, and evaluation interface unchanged. This controlled setup enables direct comparison between one-shot generation and inference-time adaptive refinement, isolating the effect of self-evolution from confounding factors such as prompt variation or task reformulation.

3.3. Agent Construction

In the preceding section, we introduced a lightweight coding agent and a self-evolving coding agent as two standardized evaluation interfaces for comparing foundation models on EvoCodeBench. In this subsection, we detail how each agent is constructed, including the prompting and output-format constraints, deterministic code extraction, and the submission-and-feedback loop with the online judge. We then describe the within-inference reflection–revision procedure used by the self-evolving agent, enabling analysis under the same task specification and scoring protocol.

Coding Agent. As illustrated in Appendix C.1.3, the coding agent is deliberately designed to be lightweight and minimally augmented. It receives as input a standardized prompt consisting of the problem statement and a language-specific starter template, and it instructs the model to produce a format-constrained response with two explicit fields. The reasoning field contains the model’s intermediate reasoning, while the code field contains the final solution expressed in the provided template format. The agent deterministically extracts the code field and submits it to the online judge for execution-based evaluation. Importantly, this baseline agent operates in a single-pass manner and does not incorporate external memory, tool use, or iterative refinement. Both the prompting schema and the output parsing rules are fixed across models, ensuring that observed performance differences can be attributed to the underlying model capabilities rather than agent-level augmentation or inference-time adaptation.

Self-evolving Coding Agent. To evaluate inference-time self-evolution, we design a self-evolving coding agent that performs controlled, within-inference refinement of solution code. Starting from an initial model-generated draft, the agent iteratively improves the solution through a fixed-budget sequence of reflection and revision steps within a single problem-solving episode. At each iteration, the agent prompts the model to analyze its current solution and identify potential failure modes, including unhandled corner cases, logical errors, suboptimal complexity, or language-specific issues. Based on this analysis, the model proposes targeted code revisions aimed at improving correctness or efficiency. The updated solution is then resubmitted to the online judge, and execution feedback is recorded. Crucially, only the solution artifact is modified during self-evolution. The problem specification, prompt schema, evaluation interface, and model parameters remain fixed, ensuring that observed gains are attributable solely to inference-time refinement rather than changes in task formulation or external augmentation. By constraining refinement to a single inference episode with a fixed revision budget, this agent enables systematic analysis of improvement trajectories in both correctness and efficiency.

4. Empirical Studies

4.1. Experimental Settings

Benchmark Settings. We construct the evaluation set by sampling 100 problems from the full collection of 3,822 tasks, spanning diverse tag categories to cover a broad range of algorithmic skills. We avoid evaluating on the full pool because widely circulated LeetCode problems, particularly older ones, may overlap with the training data of commonly used LLMs. Such overlap can inflate measured performance and confound comparisons through memorization. We therefore focus on a recent set of 100 problems as a held out test set to reduce the risk of data leakage while preserving topical diversity. We evaluate models in five programming languages. We include widely used languages such as Python3, C++, Java, and Go, and we additionally include Kotlin as a representative long tail language. This choice enables analysis of cross-language robustness under skewed language popularity and quantifies performance shifts when moving from high- to lower-resource settings.

LLMs Settings. We evaluate a set of frontier models, including deepseek-v3.2, grok-4.1-fast, gemini-3-flash-preview, gemini-3-pro-preview, claude-sonnet-4.5, claude-opus-4.5 and gpt-5.2. For all models, we enable reasoning by default. The maximum number of generated tokens to 65,536 for each response.

Agent Settings. We use the coding agent without additional agent level constraints beyond the standardized prompting and parsing protocol. For the self-evolving coding agent, we allow at most three reflection and revision iterations per problem.

4.2. Evaluation Metrics

We report three groups of metrics that capture complementary aspects of coding performance. First, capability metrics measure functional correctness and failure modes under the judge constraints. Second, efficiency metrics summarize runtime and memory cost for accepted submissions. Third, human metrics quantify how often accepted submissions outperform the distribution of human solutions in runtime and memory.

Coding capability metrics.

  • •

    Pass Rate (PR): The number of problems that the model successfully passed all test cases within the time and memory limits.

  • •

    Time Limit Exceeded (TLE): The number of problems where the model’s solution exceeded the allowed execution time limit.

  • •

    Memory Limit Exceeded (MLE): The number of problems where the model’s solution exceeded the allowed memory usage.

  • •

    Compile Error (CE): The number of problems where the model’s generated code failed to compile due to syntax errors.

  • •

    Runtime Error (RE): The number of problems where the model’s solution encountered a runtime error during execution.

  • •

    Wrong Answer (WA): The number of problems where the model’s solution produced incorrect output for the test cases.

  • •

    Timeout (TO): The number of problems where the model failed to generate a response within the specified timeout period.

  • •

    Response Error (RpE): The number of problems where the model failed to return a valid or parseable code response.

Coding efficiency metrics.

  • •

    Average Runtime (AR): The average execution runtime in milliseconds of the model’s accepted solutions across all problems.

  • •

    Average Memory (AM): The average memory consumption in megabytes of the model’s accepted solutions across all problems.

  • •

    Average Passed Cases (APC): The average number of test cases that the model’s solutions successfully passed before failure.

Human-referenced metrics.

  • •

    Average Runtime Beats (ARB): The percentage of accepted solutions where the model’s runtime performance beats other human submissions.

  • •

    Average Memory Beats (AMB): The percentage of accepted solutions where the model’s memory beats human submissions.

4.3. Overall Comparison of Models

Table 1 and Figure 3 report the main results of EvoCodeBench across languages. The results are analyzed along three complementary dimensions: coding capability, efficiency, and human-referenced comparison. The empirical analysis are as follows:

4.3.1. Comparison of Coding Capability

We begin by analyzing pass rates together with detailed error profiles across programming languages, which jointly provide a diagnostic view of both solution quality and language-level execution robustness under heterogeneous constraints. In Figure 3, this dimension corresponds to the first row, which plots within-inference pass-rate trajectories as problems accumulate.

Finding 1. Model performance degrades systematically from high-resource to long-tail languages, indicating limited robustness to language coverage. gpt-5.2 consistently emerges as the strongest performer in high-resource settings, achieving the highest pass rates in Python3, C++, Java, and Go, with PR values of 84, 90, 91, and 90, respectively. Notably, it is the only model to exceed a pass rate of 90 in Java. Figure 3 corroborates this advantage in the first row by showing that gpt-5.2 sustains one of the highest PR trajectories across these languages throughout the task sequence. However, its performance degrades in the long-tail language Kotlin, where the pass rate drops to 78. This degradation coincides with a sharp rise in compilation errors, with CE increasing to 17. More broadly, the first-row trajectories show that nearly all models experience a downward shift when moving from high-resource languages to Kotlin, indicating a structural robustness gap that persists even for top performers.

Finding 2. Performance degradation in second-tier models is primarily driven by code-level errors rather than algorithmic misunderstanding. The three models claude-4.5-opus, gemini-3-flash-preview, and gemini-3-pro-preview form a competitive cluster that achieves pass rates primarily in the 70 to high-80 range across languages. Their performance gap relative to gpt-5.2 is small in Python3 but becomes more pronounced in compiled languages. In these settings, compilation errors increase noticeably, particularly in Go and Kotlin. Importantly, wrong-answer rates within this tier remain relatively stable across languages, which suggests that the dominant bottleneck is not a wholesale collapse in algorithm selection. Instead, failures are better explained by language-specific implementation friction, such as syntax details, library and API usage, and toolchain constraints that prevent otherwise plausible solutions from executing correctly. This highlights that in compiled and long-tail languages, executability and correctness are tightly coupled, and code-level robustness can dominate observed performance even when high-level solution ideas are similar.

Finding 3. Evaluations restricted to high-resource languages can substantially overestimate the true coding capability of some models. grok-4.1-fast maintains pass rates in the high 60 to low 70 for Python3, C++, and Java, but shows a marked decline in Go and Kotlin, with pass rates dropping to 69 and 62, respectively. This decline is accompanied by elevated compilation error rates of 16 in Go and 22 in Kotlin. These results support the hypothesis that long-tail languages expose weaknesses in code generation robustness that are not apparent when evaluation is restricted to Python-centric benchmarks.

Finding 4. Algorithmic inefficiency emerges as a distinct failure mode that is not captured by pass rate alone. The model claude-4.5-sonnet demonstrates consistently low pass rates across all languages, hovering around the low 40. In contrast to other models, its failures are dominated by time limit exceeded errors rather than compilation or response errors, with TLE counts exceeding 35 in every language evaluated. This indicates that the model frequently produces syntactically valid and executable code, but struggles to select or implement algorithms that meet the required efficiency constraints. Such behavior underscores the importance of explicitly separating functional correctness from algorithmic efficiency in the evaluation of coding systems, since execution-based benchmarks must account not only for whether a solution is correct, but also for whether it meets the computational constraints for practical deployment.

Finding 5. Severe output format violations in some models reveal weaknesses in structured code generation. The model deepseek-v3.2 performs worst overall, exhibiting severe response errors across all languages. RpE counts exceed 35 in every setting and are further compounded by substantial compilation errors in C++, Java, and Go. These failures undermine execution-based evaluation and reveal weaknesses in output format compliance and instruction adherence, independent of algorithmic difficulty.

In conclusion, our results highlight that multilingual robustness, efficiency under judge constraints, and structured output reliability are all first-order factors for LLM-based coding systems. To improve performance, models should strengthen long-tail language competence through targeted multilingual training and toolchain-aware code generation that reduces compilation and execution-blocking errors. They should incorporate explicit efficiency reasoning and optimization to avoid time-limit failures, and adopt schema-constrained decoding and validation to prevent response-format violations that preclude execution-based evaluation. These directions are complementary and directly motivated by the failure patterns exposed by EvoCodeBench, reflecting practical limitations observed across languages and execution settings.

4.3.2. Comparison of Coding Efficiency

We next examine efficiency using the three columns in Table 1 that summarize average runtime, average memory, and average passed cases. These metrics quantify the computational cost of accepted solutions and the depth of progress when solutions fail. In Figure 3, the second row plots cumulative runtime as tasks accumulate. Lower curves indicate stronger end-to-end efficiency under the judge interface because time limit exceeded outcomes incur penalties and therefore increase accumulated cost.

Finding 1. Differences in end-to-end efficiency are primarily driven by the stability of solution executability. In the second row of Figure 3, gpt-5.2 consistently maintains the lowest or near-lowest cumulative runtime across all languages. This reflects not only fast accepted solutions but, more importantly, a high success rate with very few penalties from compilation or execution failures. Models such as gemini-3-pro-preview, gemini-3-flash-preview, and claude-4.5-opus initially track closely to the best-performing curve, but as tasks accumulate, particularly in Go and Kotlin, cumulative differences gradually emerge due to slightly lower executability, which results in more frequent failure penalties. In contrast, claude-4.5-sonnet and deepseek-v3.2 show much steeper cumulative runtime growth, dominated by timeout penalties, even when some solutions are relatively fast. These observations indicate that stable end-to-end efficiency is primarily determined by the model’s ability to reliably produce executable solutions, and cumulative runtime effectively amplifies differences in executability across models.

Finding 2. Among high pass-rate models, conditional runtime and memory still exhibit substantial implementation-level differences. Average runtime and average memory are computed only over accepted submissions and therefore characterize conditional efficiency among solved problems. Among higher pass-rate models, gpt-5.2 achieves competitive runtimes in compiled languages, with 228.62 ms in C++, 160.32 ms in Java, and 162.16 ms in Go, while gemini-3-pro-preview attains the lowest average runtime among the stronger models in Python3 at 1112.49 ms. Memory exhibits a different structure. Java and C++ typically have larger memory footprints while Go is often lower and Kotlin falls in between, reflecting runtime-system differences. Within a fixed language, however, models still vary substantially in average memory, suggesting that implementation choices such as data structure selection and allocation patterns materially affect efficiency beyond correctness.

Finding 3. Failures are not homogeneous: average passed cases reveal the stage at which solutions break down. Average passed cases tends to remain high for frontier models across languages, indicating that many failures occur after passing a large portion of hidden tests and are consistent with late-stage corner cases. When response errors or severe compilation issues occur, average passed cases can drop and indicates early breakdowns that prevent deep test coverage. deepseek-v3.2 illustrates this behavior in Java where average passed cases drops to 481.45, consistent with its unstable execution outcomes. This metric is complementary to cumulative runtime because it helps explain whether penalties arise from early pipeline failures or from solutions that are close to acceptance but miss a small set of cases.

In conclusion, efficiency differences in EvoCodeBench are shaped by penalty-accumulating runtime trajectories and by the conditional runtime, memory, and failure depth of accepted and near-miss solutions. This suggests actionable guidance for coding agents that goes beyond correctness. Agents should perform complexity-aware planning before coding, apply targeted revisions that replace high-cost approaches when time-limit signals appear, and explicitly trade off runtime and memory via data-structure choices. When failures occur, average passed cases help distinguish early breakdowns from late-stage corner-case errors, enabling more efficient refinement under fixed budgets.

4.3.3. Comparison of Human-referenced Performance

We evaluate human-referenced efficiency with ARB and AMB, which correspond to average runtime beats and average memory beats against the empirical distribution of human submissions for the same problem and programming language. In Figure 3, this dimension corresponds to the third row, which tracks cumulative averages of runtime beats and memory beats as tasks accumulate. The solid and dotted trajectories therefore indicate whether competitiveness against humans is stable over the task sequence, rather than being driven by a small subset of early and easy problems.

Finding 1. Strong models sustain human-competitive efficiency across languages, and this competitiveness persists over the task sequence. Across languages, frontier models typically achieve ARB and AMB above 50, indicating that their accepted solutions are often faster and more memory efficient than a majority of human submissions. This pattern is most pronounced for gpt-5.2, which maintains consistently strong third-row trajectories and reaches particularly high values in Kotlin, with ARB 88.44 and AMB 83.12. claude-4.5-opus, gemini-3-flash-preview, and gemini-3-pro-preview also attain high beats in several languages, and their third-row curves remain relatively stable as more tasks accumulate. This suggests that human-competitive efficiency is not limited to a small number of easy problems, but is maintained across a broader slice of the benchmark.

Finding 2. Human-referenced beats decouple conditional efficiency from benchmark coverage. Because ARB and AMB are defined only for accepted submissions, a model with low pass rate can still appear strong in beats if its few successful solutions are unusually efficient. For example, deepseek-v3.2 attains a low pass rate of 11 in C++, yet its accepted submissions achieve ARB 73.11 and AMB 74.05. This selection effect is also visible in the third row, where some trajectories remain moderate even when the corresponding pass-rate curve is low. As a result, beats metrics quantify conditional efficiency among solved cases, while pass rate measures coverage, and the two should be interpreted jointly when comparing models.

Finding 3. The gap between runtime beats and memory beats reveals distinct tradeoffs relative to human solutions. In some settings, models achieve much higher ARB than AMB, indicating solutions that prioritize speed over memory compared to human submissions. For instance, in Python3 gpt-5.2 attains ARB 68.06 but AMB 37.98, suggesting stronger relative runtime competitiveness than memory competitiveness. In other settings, ARB and AMB are closer, indicating more balanced efficiency. The solid and dotted third-row trajectories make these tradeoffs visible as tasks accumulate, complementing absolute runtime and memory statistics with an interpretable human-referenced scale.

In conclusion, ARB and AMB together with the third-row trajectories in Figure 3 show that human-competitive efficiency can be sustained across tasks, yet it interacts with both benchmark coverage and runtime–memory tradeoffs. This suggests practical guidance for coding agents. Agents should optimize for beats only after securing correctness, choose a speed–memory tradeoff matching problem constraints, and report beats jointly with pass rate to avoid over-interpreting efficiency from few accepted cases.

4.4. Evaluation for Self-Evolving Agents

Self-evolving coding agents aim to improve solution quality and efficiency during a single inference process through iterative refinement. Existing code benchmarks typically evaluate only the final submission and therefore provide limited visibility into when and how such within-inference self-evolution helps. EvoCodeBench supports a more fine-grained evaluation because it exposes execution outcomes, partial progress signals, and efficiency statistics, enabling trajectory-level analyses in addition to endpoint scores. In what follows, we evaluate self-evolving agents from two complementary perspectives. We first summarize overall performance using the same standardized metrics as in the main results. We then study within-inference evolution trajectories across reflection and revision steps to quantify improvement dynamics.

4.4.1. Self-Evolving Performance

Coding capability. Table 2 compares a vanilla coding agent against an evolving variant for gemini-3-flash-preview. Across languages, the evolving agent yields relative pass-rate improvements of 10.1 to 26.7 percent. Figure 4 corroborates this in the first row by showing consistently higher pass-rate trajectories as tasks accumulate. The effect is strongest in compiled languages, where pass rates reach 99 in C++ and 98 in Java. These improvements are accompanied by broad reductions in execution blocking errors. Compilation error, runtime error, timeout, and response error frequently drop to zero, indicating that iterative refinement effectively repairs format and tooling issues. Beyond executability, the evolving agent also reduces algorithmic failures. Time limit exceeded and wrong answer counts decrease substantially, suggesting that self reflection helps identify inefficient approaches and missed corner cases. Overall, within inference refinement can convert many near miss submissions into accepted solutions under the same evaluation interface.

Coding efficiency. Efficiency metrics show that the evolving agent improves runtime in every language, with average runtime decreasing by 7.8 percent in Python3 and by 19.8 to 46.4 percent in compiled languages. In Figure 4, the second row confirms this trend, as the evolving agent accumulates substantially lower cumulative runtime and the gap widens as tasks accumulate. This pattern is consistent with reductions in time limit exceeded errors and suggests that evolution often replaces suboptimal algorithms with more efficient ones. Memory usage shows a mixed trend, decreasing in C++, Java, and Go but increasing modestly in Python3 and Kotlin, plausibly because the evolving agent introduces auxiliary data structures to ensure correctness or improve speed. Average passed cases changes only slightly, indicating that most gains come from turning partial solutions into fully accepted ones rather than uniformly increasing partial progress.

Human-referenced comparison. Human-referenced metrics further suggest that evolution improves human calibrated efficiency in most languages. In Figure 4, the third row shows that the evolving agent maintains higher runtime-beats and memory-beats trajectories than the vanilla agent in most settings, indicating sustained competitiveness against human submissions as tasks accumulate. Consistent with Table 2, runtime beats increase strongly in compiled languages, with ARB gains of 30.8 percent in C++ and 24.4 percent in Java, and smaller gains in Go and Kotlin. Memory beats increase in Python3, C++, Java, and Go, but decrease in Kotlin. This divergence mirrors the absolute memory trend and suggests that in long tail languages the evolving agent may trade memory for correctness or speed. Taken together, these results indicate that EvoCodeBench can quantify not only endpoint accuracy gains from evolution, but also whether those gains align with human efficiency distributions over the inference trajectory.

4.4.2. Within-Inference Evolution Trajectories

Figure 4 illustrates how EvoCodeBench enables trajectory-level evaluation of self-evolving coding agents. In the first row, the evolving agent maintains consistently higher pass-rate trajectories across languages, indicating that improvements persist as problems accumulate. In the second row, the evolving agent exhibits substantially lower cumulative runtime, with the widening gap suggesting compounding efficiency gains from fewer penalties and faster solutions. In the third row, the evolving agent sustains higher runtime-beats and memory-beats trajectories, showing that accepted solutions become more competitive relative to humans as inference progresses. Together, these signals complement endpoint metrics by revealing when and how within-inference refinement improves correctness and efficiency.

5. Conclusion

We introduced EvoCodeBench, a multilingual, execution based benchmark for evaluating LLM based coding systems under a unified online judge protocol. EvoCodeBench jointly measures error modes, resource efficiency, and human referential competitiveness, enabling comparisons that remain meaningful across high resource and long tail languages. Our results reveal systematic performance degradation in long tail languages, distinct failure modes driven by code level robustness and algorithmic inefficiency, and substantial variation in structured output reliability. We further demonstrate that EvoCodeBench supports within inference evaluation of self evolving agents by exposing improvement trajectories in pass rate, cumulative runtime, and beats metrics. We hope EvoCodeBench will facilitate more reliable evaluation and drive progress toward coding agents that are robust across languages, efficient under constraints, and competitive with human solutions.

Appendix A Code and Data Availability

All code and data will be publicly available upon acceptance of this paper, including the benchmark query set, evaluation pipeline, backtest engine, and supplementary scripts for reproducing the reported results.

Appendix B Motivation

The design of EvoCodeBench is driven by three complementary observations about the current evaluation landscape for LLM-based coding systems. In this section, we elaborate on each motivation in detail and explain how our benchmark addresses the corresponding gap.

B.1. Evaluating Inference-Time Self-Evolution

A growing body of work explores how LLM-based agents can improve during inference through iterative refinement, self-repair, and reflection (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023). In the coding domain, these systems refine candidate solutions by analyzing execution feedback, diagnosing failure modes such as wrong answers or time-limit violations, and producing revised implementations within a single problem-solving episode. This inference-time self-evolution has been shown to substantially boost pass rates, sometimes surpassing the performance of stronger base models operating in a single-pass mode (Olausson et al., 2023).

Despite the growing importance of such systems, existing code benchmarks are not designed to characterize this behavior. They evaluate only the final submitted solution and report a single correctness score, which collapses all intermediate dynamics into one number. As a result, they cannot answer questions such as: Does the system become more accurate as it iterates? Does efficiency improve alongside correctness, or does the system trade runtime for correctness? How many revision rounds are needed before gains saturate? These trajectory-level questions are critical for understanding self-evolving agents, yet they require benchmarks that expose per-iteration feedback signals, including execution outcomes, runtime, memory, and partial-progress indicators.

EvoCodeBench addresses this gap by recording the full sequence of submissions, execution verdicts, and resource statistics across reflection and revision steps. This enables trajectory-level analyses that separate one-shot generation quality from inference-time adaptation gains, quantify the speed and cost of improvement, and identify when self-evolution helps versus when it introduces regressions. Our empirical results confirm that this design reveals meaningful improvement dynamics. For example, the self-evolving agent achieves pass-rate improvements of 10 to 27 percent relative to the vanilla agent, and cumulative runtime decreases substantially as tasks accumulate, indicating compounding efficiency gains that would be invisible under endpoint-only evaluation.

B.2. Calibrating Performance Against Human Ability

Most code benchmarks report model performance in absolute units such as pass rate or accuracy, which are difficult to interpret without an external reference frame. A pass rate of 80 conveys limited information about whether the system is approaching, matching, or exceeding typical human performance on the same tasks. This interpretability gap is especially problematic as frontier models approach high accuracy on popular benchmarks, making it unclear whether remaining failures reflect fundamental limitations or merely reflect difficult edge cases that also challenge human programmers.

Human-referenced evaluation provides a complementary perspective by locating model performance within the empirical distribution of human submissions. On platforms such as LeetCode, every accepted submission receives percentile-based statistics that indicate the fraction of human solutions it outperforms in runtime and memory. These runtime beats and memory beats metrics answer a qualitatively different question from pass rate: not just whether the model solves the problem, but how its solution compares to the solutions produced by real human programmers on the same task and in the same programming language.

EvoCodeBench integrates these human-referenced signals as first-class evaluation metrics. By reporting average runtime beats and average memory beats alongside pass rate, our benchmark enables statements such as “the model’s accepted solutions outperform 70 percent of human submissions in runtime” or “the model achieves human-competitive memory efficiency in long-tail languages despite lower pass rates.” These calibrated comparisons are essential for interpreting the practical significance of benchmark scores and for identifying settings where models are competitive with or superior to typical human programmers, which has implications for deployment decisions and trust in automated coding systems.

B.3. Assessing Cross-Language Robustness Under Long-Tail Usage

Existing code benchmarks are heavily concentrated on Python, which reflects its dominant position in both the LLM training data distribution and the developer ecosystem. According to the TIOBE Index for January 2026, Python accounts for 22.61 percent of market share, while long-tail languages such as Kotlin account for only 0.97 percent (TIOBE Software BV, 2026). This skew has two consequences for evaluation. First, benchmarks that evaluate only in Python cannot detect cross-language robustness issues, such as compilation errors in statically typed languages or API misuse in less-represented ecosystems. Second, the training data imbalance means that models are likely to have seen far fewer examples of correct Kotlin or Go code, which can translate into systematic performance degradation that single-language benchmarks would miss entirely.

Several prior efforts have extended evaluation to multiple languages (Cassano et al., 2023; Ding et al., 2023; Raihan et al., 2025), but they typically focus on translating existing Python benchmarks rather than designing evaluation protocols that explicitly target long-tail robustness. In particular, they rarely combine multilingual coverage with efficiency metrics or human-referenced comparisons, which limits their ability to diagnose whether performance gaps arise from algorithmic deficiencies, implementation-level friction, or language-specific toolchain issues.

EvoCodeBench includes five programming languages, spanning high-resource (Python3, C++, Java), moderate-resource (Go), and long-tail (Kotlin) settings, all evaluated under a unified online judge protocol with identical metrics. This design enables systematic analysis of how pass rate, error profiles, runtime, memory, and human-referenced beats shift as language resource availability decreases. Our results confirm that this multilingual design exposes robustness gaps that are invisible in Python-only evaluation: compilation errors increase sharply in long-tail languages, overall pass rates degrade systematically, and the gap between high-resource and long-tail performance varies meaningfully across models. These findings motivate the inclusion of long-tail languages as a standard component of code benchmark design.

Appendix C Case Studies

C.1. Agent Construction Details

In the main paper, we introduced two standardized evaluation interfaces: a lightweight coding agent and a self-evolving coding agent. This subsection provides additional implementation details, including prompt templates, output parsing rules, the submission pipeline, and the reflection and revision procedure.

C.1.1. Coding Agent

The coding agent is designed to be minimally augmented so that observed performance differences reflect the underlying model’s capabilities rather than agent-level engineering. Its construction follows four steps.

Step 1: Prompt Construction. For each problem and target programming language, the agent assembles a standardized prompt that consists of three components: (1) the full natural-language problem statement, including constraints and input–output examples; (2) any embedded images associated with the problem, resolved to local assets; and (3) the language-specific starter code template provided by the platform. These components are concatenated into a fixed-format input string. The prompt explicitly instructs the model to return a structured response containing two fields: a reasoning field for intermediate analysis and a code field for the final solution. This format constraint ensures deterministic parsing regardless of the model’s default output style. An illustrative prompt is shown in Appendix Figure C.1.3.

Step 2: Model Inference. The assembled prompt is sent to the target LLM with reasoning enabled by default and a maximum output token budget of 16,384 tokens. No system-level instructions, few-shot examples, or retrieval augmentation are provided. The model generates its response in a single forward pass without access to external tools, memory, or execution feedback.

Step 3: Deterministic Code Extraction. The agent parses the model’s response and extracts the content of the code field using a deterministic extraction rule. If the response does not conform to the expected format, the submission is recorded as a response error. This strict parsing ensures that evaluation failures due to format non-compliance are explicitly captured rather than silently corrected.

Step 4: Online Judge Submission and Feedback Collection. The extracted code is submitted to the LeetCode online judge for execution-based evaluation against hidden test cases. The judge returns a verdict (Accepted, Wrong Answer, Time Limit Exceeded, Memory Limit Exceeded, Compile Error, or Runtime Error), the number of passed test cases, and, for accepted submissions, runtime in milliseconds, memory usage in megabytes, and percentile-based runtime beats and memory beats statistics computed against the distribution of human submissions. All signals are recorded for downstream analysis.

C.1.2. Self-Evolving Coding Agent

The self-evolving coding agent extends the coding agent with a controlled, within-inference reflection and revision loop. Its construction adds three additional steps after the initial submission.

Step 5: Execution Feedback Analysis. After the initial submission (Steps 1–4), the agent receives the judge’s verdict and diagnostic information. If the submission is accepted, no further refinement is performed. If the submission fails, the agent constructs a reflection prompt that includes: (a) the original problem statement, (b) the previously submitted code, (c) the judge’s verdict and error details (e.g., failed test case input and expected output for wrong answers, or error messages for compile and runtime errors), and (d) an explicit instruction to analyze the failure and propose targeted improvements.

Step 6: Reflection and Revision. The model receives the reflection prompt and generates an analysis of the failure, identifying potential root causes such as unhandled corner cases, incorrect algorithmic logic, suboptimal time or space complexity, or language-specific syntax issues. Based on this analysis, the model produces a revised solution. The revised code is extracted using the same deterministic parsing rule as in Step 3 and resubmitted to the online judge.

Step 7: Iteration and Termination. Steps 5 and 6 are repeated for up to three reflection and revision rounds (configurable). The loop terminates early if any revised submission achieves an Accepted verdict. At each iteration, the full execution feedback is recorded, enabling trajectory-level analysis of how correctness, runtime, memory, and human-referenced beats evolve across revision steps.

Key Design Constraints. Throughout the self-evolution process, only the solution code is modified. The problem specification, prompt schema, evaluation interface, and model parameters remain fixed. This ensures that observed improvements are attributable solely to inference-time refinement rather than changes in task formulation, prompt engineering, or external augmentation. By constraining refinement to a fixed revision budget within a single inference episode, the agent enables reproducible analysis of improvement dynamics.

C.1.3. Prompt Example

The following case study illustrates the prompt format used by the coding agent. The input includes the problem statement, examples with visual illustrations, constraints, and the language-specific starter template.

C.1.4. Self-Evolving Coding Agent Prompts

The self-evolving coding agent uses two types of reflection prompts depending on the judge verdict: a bugfix reflection when the submission fails and an optimization reflection when the submission is accepted but performance is below a configurable threshold. The agent expects a structured JSON response with three fields: analysis, improved_reasoning, and improved_code. The reflection loop runs for at most three rounds and terminates early when the solution is accepted with competitive performance (both runtime beats and memory beats exceeding 65%). Throughout the process, only the solution code is modified; the problem specification, prompt schema, and model parameters remain fixed.

C.2. Accepted Test Cases

In this subsection, we present a representative selection of test cases where the model successfully generated correct solutions, achieving an “Accepted” status. These examples demonstrate the agent’s proficiency in handling a diverse range of data structures and algorithmic paradigms, specifically focusing on arrays, math, dynamic programming and graph theory. Through these cases, we illustrate the model’s capability to interpret complex logic, implement efficient algorithms (such as monotonic stacks and bitwise operations), and satisfy strict execution constraints.

C.2.1. Case 1: Steps to Make Array Non-decreasing

In Case 1, the model addresses the problem “Steps to Make Array Non-decreasing,” a task that requires sophisticated algorithmic reasoning. A naive simulation of the removal process would result in a time complexity of O​(N2)O(N^{2}), which violates the given constraints (N=105N=10^{5}). The model successfully identifies the optimal approach using a monotonic stack, demonstrating the ability to transform a simulation problem into a linear-time O​(N)O(N) solution.

The generated explanation reveals a clear chain of thought: the model correctly deduces that an element’s removal time depends on the maximum removal time of the smaller elements it covers. By maintaining a stack of (v​a​l​u​e,t​i​m​e)(value,time) tuples, the code effectively calculates the ”collision” logic required to determine when each element is removed. The evaluation results confirm the solution’s correctness and efficiency, passing all 87 test cases and outperforming 82.5% of Python3 submissions in runtime. This case highlights the model’s capacity to handle complex state transitions and data structure optimizations without human intervention.

C.2.2. Case 2: Number of Effective Subsequences

In Case 2, the model tackles “Number of Effective Subsequences,” a problem that demands a deep understanding of combinatorial mathematics and bitwise operations. A brute-force approach iterating through all subsequences would yield a time complexity of O​(2N)O(2^{N}), which is computationally infeasible. The model successfully identifies that this is a counting problem best solved using the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion (PIE) combined with Sum Over Subsets (SOS) Dynamic Programming.

The model’s inference trace demonstrates a high level of abstraction: it correctly formulates the problem as finding the number of subsets that maintain the full bitwise OR sum, and then subtracting this from the total. It employs an optimization technique—mapping the active bits of the total OR sum to a compact range—to minimize the SOS DP state space to O​(d⋅2d)O(d\cdot 2^{d}), where dd is the number of set bits (at most 20). The evaluation results (1041/1041 cases passed) and the high efficiency ranking (beating 71.26% of submissions) validate the model’s ability to implement complex mathematical algorithms correctly.

C.2.3. Case 3: Remove Methods From Project

In Case 3, the model solves “Remove Methods From Project,” a graph theory problem involving reachability analysis and constraint verification. The solution requires a two-step logic: first, identifying the connected component of “suspicious” nodes starting from node kk, and second, validating that no external nodes invoke any node within this component.

The model correctly decomposes the problem, employing a standard Breadth-First Search (BFS) to mark all reachable nodes from the source kk. Crucially, it recognizes the necessity of a post-traversal validation step: iterating through the edge list to detect if any “safe” node directs to a “suspicious” node, which is the failure condition for removal. The implementation is highly optimized, using an adjacency list for traversal and a boolean array for state tracking, resulting in linear time complexity O​(V+E)O(V+E). The evaluation confirms the efficiency of this approach, with the generated code outperforming 99.38% of Python3 submissions.

C.3. Compile Error Resolution via Reflection Agent

This case exemplifies the capability of the Reflection Agent to handle language-specific syntax errors that prevent code execution. The model initially formulated a correct algorithmic strategy using Dijkstra’s algorithm to solve the “Find Minimum Time to Reach Last Room I” problem. However, the submission failed with a Compile Error due to an ambiguous import of PriorityQueue in the Kotlin environment.

Upon receiving the error signal, the Reflection Agent did not merely regenerate the code stochastically. Instead, it performed a targeted diagnosis: it identified the conflict between the explicit import and the environment’s implicit imports. Consequently, the agent refined the code by adopting a wildcard import (java.util.*) and simplifying the data structure from a custom data class to a primitive IntArray to reduce overhead. This iterative self-correction process allowed the system to recover from a fatal syntax error and achieve a fully accepted solution with competitive runtime performance.

C.4. Time Limit Exceeded Resolution via Reflection Agent

In this case, the model tackles the problem “Maximum Product of Two Integers With No Common Bits,” which involves finding an optimal pair under bitwise constraints. The initial solution correctly identified the Sum Over Subsets (SOS) DP algorithm as the standard approach to handle submask queries efficiently (O​(B⋅2B)O(B\cdot 2^{B})). However, this implementation resulted in a Time Limit Exceeded (TLE) verdict. The rejection stems from the high constant factor associated with processing 2202^{20} states and iterating through the entire array without early termination, which proved too slow for the given constraints (N=105N=10^{5}).

The Reflection Agent successfully diagnosed this performance bottleneck, recognizing that theoretical time complexity alone was insufficient. In the optimization phase, it introduced a critical heuristic: sorting and pruning. By processing unique elements in descending order, the algorithm can verify if the theoretical maximum product for the current number (current number ×\times global max) exceeds the best product found so far. This logic allows for early termination of the loop, drastically reducing the effective search space. The optimized solution, combining SOS DP with this branch-and-bound strategy, successfully passed all 762 test cases.

C.5. Wrong Answer Resolution via Reflection Agent

In this case, the model attempts to solve “Longest Special Path II,” a challenging tree traversal problem that requires maintaining a sliding window of values down a path. The constraints specify that a valid path can have distinct values with at most one value appearing twice. The initial submission resulted in a Wrong Answer (WA), failing on a specific edge case where the boundary logic for the path start index was incorrect. The model likely mishandled the complex condition of tracking multiple potential duplicate pairs simultaneously.

The Reflection Agent effectively analyzed the failure, realizing that a simple list or map was insufficient for efficiently querying the ”second-to-last” violation point. It proposed a sophisticated data structure change: using a TreeSet to store the depths of the first occurrence of every value pair currently on the recursion stack. By querying the second largest element in this set, the algorithm can instantly determine the valid starting depth of the path in O​(log⁡N)O(\log N) time. This optimization corrected the boundary logic and achieved a perfect runtime performance, beating 100% of Kotlin submissions.
